rules.condition: Late summer/early autumn estuarine yellow eels: just after sunset through night

sourceRecords.citation: Peter W. Sorensen; Marco L. Bianchini; Howard E. Winn (1986). Diel Foraging Activity of American Eels, Anguilla rostrata (LeSueur), in a Rhode Island Estuary. Fishery Bulletin 84(3):746-747.

findings: The NOAA-hosted paper directly reports overwhelmingly nocturnal baited-trap capture, with the largest fraction just after sunset.
limitations: Baited traps are not hook-and-line catch rates.
The study was conducted in a turbid Rhode Island estuary during early September and October, so the result is not a universal freshwater diel curve.

translationBlueprint.inputContract: Local solar-relative time and selected date.

validRange.season: late summer through early autumn; strongest source support is September-October
validRange.solarWindow: sunset through night, with strongest support during the first 90 minutes after sunset

translationBlueprint.proposedResponse: Use a smooth, moderate post-sunset increase and a modest daylight decrease; attenuate outside the source season and in non-estuarine waters.
translationBlueprint.missingBehavior: Neutral when local solar time cannot be calculated.
translationBlueprint.doubleCountingGuard: Use one light/diel factor; do not stack sunset, clock time, cloud, and generic nocturnal weights.

rules.nextAction: Complete source-passage review and validate the bounded evidence-informed curve before integration.

rules.condition: Progressive cooling from summer toward winter within the population's recent thermal history

sourceRecords.citation: Adam S. Nanninga, Carole R. Engle, Nathan Stone, and Andrew E. Goodwin (2011). Effects of Winter Feeding of Channel Catfish on Production in Multibatch Systems. North American Journal of Aquaculture, volume 73, issue 1, pages 60-67.

Dilip Mathur (1970). Food Habits and Feeding Chronology of Channel Catfish Ictalurus punctatus (Rafinesque), in Conowingo Reservoir. Proceedings of the Annual Conference of the Southeastern Association of Game and Fish Commissioners, volume 24, pages 377-386.

findings: The field chronology and winter-feeding experiment support continued but seasonally changing feeding, including feeding at cold temperatures.
limitations: The sources do not justify a single smooth seasonal penalty independent of acclimation, prey, and system type.
One source is a reservoir stomach-content study and the other is an aquaculture pond experiment.

translationBlueprint.evidenceClass: reservoir stomach chronology plus winter feeding experiment
translationBlueprint.inputContract: Observed or modeled water temperature and recent thermal history.

validRange.anchors: continued feeding at 7 C; progressively higher intake across <=10, 10.1-15.6, and 15.7-21.1 C

translationBlueprint.proposedResponse: Represent progressive cold-season suppression without cessation; use temperature rather than calendar month as the main driver.
translationBlueprint.missingBehavior: Fall back to the monthly seasonal prior.
translationBlueprint.doubleCountingGuard: Blend this into the single seasonal-thermal factor; do not multiply monthly winter and cold-water penalties.

rules.condition: Sustained cyclic water temperature reaching 31-35 C (87.8-95 F)

sourceRecords.citation: Michael B. Arnold, Eugene L. Torrans, and Peter J. Allen (2013). Influences of Cyclic, High Temperatures on Juvenile Channel Catfish Growth and Feeding. North American Journal of Aquaculture, volume 75, issue 1, pages 77-84.

findings: The USDA record confirms lower feed consumption, growth, and survival in the hottest 31-35 C cyclic treatment.
limitations: The experiment used juvenile channel catfish in aquaculture tanks, so the result supports a severe-heat guardrail more directly than a field catchability curve.

translationBlueprint.inputContract: Observed or modeled water temperature plus recent heat-exposure history.
translationBlueprint.proposedResponse: Apply no separate bonus at 27-31 C; increase the existing high-temperature penalty only as sustained conditions enter 31-35 C.
translationBlueprint.missingBehavior: Neutral beyond the ordinary thermal factor when heat history is unavailable.
translationBlueprint.doubleCountingGuard: Replace the high-temperature tail of the thermal curve and ignore stress-related tank activity as positive catchability.

rules.condition: Chronic or acclimated conditions near 6 C versus 14-28 C
rules.direction: strong negative at 6 C; higher at intermediate/warm treatments

sourceRecords.citation: Chen Song-bo; Chen Wei-xing; Fan Zhao-ting (2012). Effect of Water Temperature on Feeding Rhythm in Common Carp (Cyprinus carpio haematopterus Temminck et Schlegel). Journal of Northeast Agricultural University (English Edition) 19(1):57-61.

findings: The publisher abstract reports very low feeding at 6 C, increasing feeding through intermediate treatments, a maximum at 28 C, and a decrease at 34 C.
limitations: Only the publisher abstract was available in this preflight.
The controlled aquaculture population and feeding protocol do not directly establish NOVA angling catchability.

translationBlueprint.inputContract: Observed or modeled water temperature in degrees C.

validRange.anchors: very low at 6 C, higher by 14 C, highest highlighted treatment at 28 C, lower at 34 C

translationBlueprint.proposedResponse: Fit a conservative shape through the four observed anchors without treating 28 C as a universal field optimum or extrapolating outside 6-34 C.
translationBlueprint.missingBehavior: Fall back to seasonal activity when water temperature is unavailable.
translationBlueprint.doubleCountingGuard: Replace the existing thermal response; do not stack cold and warm carp rules separately.

rules.condition: May-June tidal Potomac: daylight, especially morning, versus overnight

sourceRecords.citation: Nicolas W. R. Lapointe; Ryan K. Saylor; Paul L. Angermeier (2019). Diel Feeding and Movement Activity of Northern Snakehead Channa argus. Proceedings of the First International Snakehead Symposium, AFS Symposium 89:69-81.

findings: The primary Potomac study reports little fresh prey overnight and greater feeding in morning/daylight samples during May and June.
limitations: The diel model explained only a small share of feeding variation.
The result must remain limited to the tidal Potomac and the sampled May-June season unless new evidence supports transfer.

translationBlueprint.evidenceClass: local tidal-river field feeding and movement study
translationBlueprint.inputContract: Local solar-relative time and selected date.

validRange.waterbody: tidal Potomac and comparable tidal river habitat

translationBlueprint.proposedResponse: Apply a bounded morning/daylight increase and overnight decrease in May-June; strongly attenuate outside the source season or tidal setting.
translationBlueprint.missingBehavior: Neutral without local solar time or location scope.
translationBlueprint.doubleCountingGuard: Use one diel/tide joint cap so daylight and outgoing tide cannot independently reach full strength.

rules.nextAction: Human source sign-off, bounded curve design, adversarial tests, and held-out validation.

rules.condition: Dawn/dusk or lower measured solar radiation in a lake fishery

sourceRecords.citation: Stephanie L. Shaw; Kathryn M. Renik; Greg G. Sass (2021). Angler and environmental influences on walleye Sander vitreus and muskellunge Esox masquinongy angler catch in Escanaba Lake, Wisconsin 2003-2015. PLOS ONE 16(9):e0257882.

findings: The long-term compulsory-creel study directly estimated higher walleye angling success at dawn and dusk than during daytime and a negative solar-radiation effect.
limitations: The effect comes from one Wisconsin lake fishery and requires conservative transfer to NOVA lakes and reservoirs.
Solar radiation and diel period are correlated and must not be scored twice.

translationBlueprint.inputContract: Local solar-relative period and optionally forecast surface solar radiation for lake/reservoir locations.
translationBlueprint.proposedResponse: Apply bounded dawn and dusk increases relative to day, with radiation as an alternate continuous representation rather than an additional factor.
translationBlueprint.missingBehavior: Use solar-relative period alone when radiation is missing; otherwise neutral.
translationBlueprint.doubleCountingGuard: Dawn/dusk, cloud, and solar radiation are one latent light signal and cannot stack.

rules.nextAction: Human source sign-off, bounded curve design, adversarial tests, and held-out validation.
